label: Person
name: Agustín Parrado y García
summary:
Agustín Parrado y García (1863–1946) was a Spanish Catholic archbishop who served as Archbishop of Granada and later as Archbishop of Seville, occupying the two most historically prestigious sees in Andalusia. Born in Baena, he rose through the Spanish ecclesiastical hierarchy to lead the ancient archdioceses associated with Moorish, Jewish, and Christian cultural heritage.

Parrado y García served through one of Spain's most turbulent periods: the Restoration monarchy, the collapse of the constitutional monarchy, the Second Republic, and the Spanish Civil War. His long tenure at Seville (1929–1946) coincided with the Civil War, during which the Church in nationalist-controlled Andalusia largely aligned with Franco's forces and suffered significant persecution in Republican-held areas. Seville, firmly in nationalist hands from 1936, became a stronghold of Catholic conservative culture during the war.

His archiepiscopate at both Granada and Seville connected him to the deepest layers of Spanish Catholic history: Granada's Cathedral housed the tombs of Ferdinand and Isabella; Seville's Cathedral was the largest Gothic church in the world and the site of Christopher Columbus's tomb. Leading these ancient sees required a figure of ecclesiastical dignity capable of representing the Church in settings saturated with national-religious memory.
